b8815ba3de8be9e28e5b3a87703e1e35.text: Vanessa Moberg is the Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society's financial coordinator. After some recent decluttering Vanessa Moberg still kept a bag of tar sands, a sentimental reminder of her uncle and a practical reminder of the fossil fuels required to produce all her other stuff. Eager to declutter, I recently went through my boxes of sentimental items. “I’m a minimalist,” I thought. “This should be easy.” Before long, I found myself holding a Ziploc bag filled with a dark substance, and I thought, “Oh yeah! The tar sands my uncle gave me. Well, I can’t just throw out these perfectly good tar sands, now, can I?” I spent most of that day sitting on the basement floor surrounded by my “thing piles”: keep, store, donate, recycle. It was a thoroughly exhausting day filled with micro-decisions. Somehow, we develop a strong emotional attachment to a thing, even as the thing holds absolutely no purpose in our lives. We may remember buying it, how proud we were of it, the effort it took to acquire it, or the hopes we had for it. When we hold the thing in our hands again, all those emotions come flooding back, and we hesitate to get rid of it, even though it has spent the last decade relegated to a box, at the back of a closet, in the room no one goes into. There are health implications of having too many things. Studies have linked clutter to sleep disturbances, digestive problems, poor food choices, and even relationship issues. On the other hand, having clean, minimalist spaces can make one feel light, relaxed, organized, and more productive. Beyond the mental health effects, it takes a financial toll, not just to acquire things, but to maintain, insure, and store them. And then there are the environmental effects. Aside from the obvious end-of-life waste generated, most things require surprising amounts of resources to produce, transport, operate, and throw away, including water, chemicals, raw materials, and energy – often fossil fuels. af19f098f3c398d6344ec5be40d001cf.text: 100 Mile Ford is collecting coats and other winter wear this month. 100 Mile Ford is on track to raise over 100 jackets for community members in need this winter. For the past several weeks, 100 Mile Ford has been taking part in the KOT Auto Group’s eighth annual Coat Drive, the third time the dealership has participated. Carole Velne, an accountant with 100 Mile Ford, said they are looking to collect as many coats, gloves, toques and other winter accessories as possible. “For those that need a little bit more extra warmth at this time of year. We collect coats, hats, toques, mitts and scarves,” Velne said. “We pile them up into our truck and at the end of November they will all be taken out to the Cariboo Christian Life Fellowship (CCLF) church in the 108 Mile Ranch area.” As of Wednesday, Nov. 18, Velne said the Ford Ranger they’ve been storing the donations in is half full. She noted that they would welcome more donations to come in for the last few days of November. To donate, Velne said community members simply need to come by 100 Mile Ford during their regular hours of operation and drop off their donations. She noted that some have left bags of clothes by the front door when they come in to work in the morning. “We know times are tough. The economy is not booming the best right now. There’s just a lot of people out there who really can’t afford the proper warm jackets for the Cariboo weather up here,” Velne said. “Whatever little bit people can throw our way is just such a big help.” Donations will be accepted until Monday, Nov. 30. Afterwards, they’ll go to the CCLF, which will be responsible for distributing them. Velne said she is looking forward to seeing just how much winter wear they can raise. “I think whatever people have that would keep people warm would be gladly accepted.” **News** **Doerkson lays out immediate priorities, explains B.C. cabinet

e787c671119014dcfc68c88548768019.text: If your period home is heated by oil or LPG and isn’t connected to mains gas, you could currently be eligible for up to £9,000 towards an air-source or ground-source heat pump – an appealing prospect with temperatures plummeting and winter drawing near. But the additional £1,500 grant is only available until March 2027 – and if you leave the decision until your boiler breaks in the middle of winter, you may not have time to make use of it. A heat pump is not a quick replacement. Your home needs to be surveyed, the system designed around its heat loss and existing pipework, and changes such as larger radiators or a bigger hot-water cylinder may be recommended. That makes November a crucial moment to start the process. As Lewis Harding, a Gas Safe registered engineer at First Point Plumbing in New Mills, explains: "Make the call in the autumn, while the old oil boiler still runs. Once it gives out in January, most families order whatever can go in that week, because nobody wants to sit in a cold farmhouse while a heat pump is planned around the house." In other words, the grant deadline and the boiler deadline are working against each other. Wait for a midwinter breakdown and you could find yourself choosing the fastest available boiler instead, but start now, and you have time to establish whether a heat pump is suitable, compare installers and apply for the funding. Here's how to get going... An old stone farmhouse or barn conversion needs a system designed around its quirks. A survey should assess how much heat each room loses, check the existing pipework and radiators, and establish whether they can keep the rooms warm with the lower water temperatures used by most heat pumps. Some radiators may need replacing with larger models and a new hot-water cylinder could be needed. Listed buildings bring another consideration. 1de13f6f28c972b9dda1ab35f09238a7.text: In the wake of the Bald Range wildfire, an international study is seeking volunteers from the South Okanagan for a new treatment method for those dealing with post-traumatic stress disorder. Penticton in the South Okanagan is one of four B.C. communities, alongside Kelowna, Kamloops and North Vancouver, selected to participate in the study. The impacts of the Bald Range wildfire, which saw thousands of people forced out of their homes in the Okanagan, left behind more than physical scars on the region. About 150 structures, including homes and accessory structures, were destroyed within the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen and District of Summerland as a result of the fast-moving Aug. 7 blaze. Faulder was particularly hard hit by the fire, as the closest community to the origin point. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. “PTSD touches so many people in our community: first responders, people who’ve survived accidents or violence, families who lost homes to fire. Being part of rigorous, closely supervised research means people in the South Okanagan have a real voice in what the next generation of care looks like,” said Dr. Linda Grasswick, principal investigator for the study in Penticton. Medical Arts Health Research Group is conducting the study under Health Canada and research ethics oversight. The treatment will explore an investigational form of psilocybin, one of the naturally occurring compounds found in many so-called “magic” mushrooms. Adults living with PTSD in the South Okanagan who would like to learn more can contact the study team confidentially at (888) 490-4320 or visit www.healthresearch.ca. Reaching out does not commit anyone to participate. Those interested will be screened by a doctor to determine whether the study is a safe and appropriate fit. Participants will receive care and support from a dedicated study team throughout, and study-related visits, assessments, and the investigational medication are provided at no cost.

Courtney McCowan's family is seeking answers after she died outside of Port Hardy Hospital on Nov. 19. The family of a 48-year-old woman who died outside Port Hardy Hospital on Nov. 19 is seeking answers. Courtney McCowan was treated by paramedics for an estimated 39 minutes outside the hospital’s doors before she passed away, according to her daughter, Hailey Schubert (That timeline is unconfirmed). “Apparently she got there at 5:11 (p.m.),” Schubert said. “So 11 minutes after they had closed. Her friend tried to get her into (the) emergency (department). They denied her. They wouldn’t let her in.” Schubert said a paramedic was in the parking lot cleaning an ambulance and noticed what was happening: “So, he came over to attend to my mom, and started doing CPR. They had called 911, so then two other ambulances from a nearby ambulance station came over to help.” According to Schubert, at this point, no one from the hospital was letting them in. “At that point, 39 minutes later, for whatever reason, they changed their minds and they decided to let her in, but by that point it was too late.” In a statement, B.C. Minister of Health Ryan Peterson said, “Our thoughts are with the family members and loved ones impacted by the tragic outcome that happened on the grounds of the Port Hardy Hospital on Thursday (Nov. 19).” The Ministry noted that Island Health and BC Emergency Health Services are investigating the circumstances of this incident. “What we know at this time is that both Island Health care providers and BCEHS paramedics responded and provided emergency interventions,” Peterson added. “Access to health care is one of our government’s top priorities. 980e89f1cefd532da0a68ec27e65a18c.text: Visitors to Barkerville during its Olde-Fashioned Christmas weekend can experience traditional sleigh rides through the historic site. Anyone looking for a very special Christmas adventure, as well as a trip back in time, can experience both during Barkerville Historic Town & Park’s Olde-Fashioned Christmas, which takes place from Dec. 11–13. The celebration allows visitors to enjoy the sights and sounds of Christmas past in one of British Columbia’s most iconic historic settings: Barkerville. Located approximately 80 kilometres east of Quesnel, the town was born when Billy Barker struck gold on Williams Creek in 1862. Today, the National Historic Site brings the Gold Rush era to life through more than 125 heritage buildings, exhibits, demonstrations, and costumed performers in a spectacular setting. Barkerville’s Olde-Fashioned Christmas festivities begin on Friday, Dec. 11, when visitors can enjoy a selection of activities, demonstrations, and shopping ahead of the weekend celebration. While not all businesses and activities will be operating on Friday, a variety of shops, exhibits, and programs will be available, allowing people to explore and enjoy the unique atmosphere of Barkerville in winter. Throughout Saturday and Sunday, visitors can enjoy carolling, guided town tours, traditional school lessons, demonstrations at the blacksmith shop and print shop, and Christmas shopping while exploring many of the town’s historic buildings and exhibits. Programming will also include Indigenous interpretation at the Kelly Hall and a holiday reading with Chartres Brew, B.C.’s first chief inspector of police who also served as gold commissioner and judge. The Correlieu Concert Band will be returning to join in the merriment on Sunday, Dec. 13. Returning favourites will also include horse-drawn sleigh rides through the historic townsite, and this year visitors will have the opportunity to book special evening sleigh rides and experience Barkerville as Christmas lights

fe57c81843c463633b34e743f7cedfcc.text: Quesnel U11 Blue Devils bring home silver from Clearwater tournament. The Quesnel U11 Blue Devils battled their way to a silver-medal finish at a 10-team tournament in Clearwater from Dec. 13-15. In an email to the *Observer,* head coach Brett Roberts said the Blue Devils opened the tournament with a pair of hard-fought victories, defeating West Kelowna 4-2 and North Okanagan 7-5. The team followed that up with a dominant 10-0 win over host Clearwater to secure second place in the round-robin standings. On Sunday morning, Quesnel faced third-place Kamloops in the semifinals, with a spot in the gold-medal game against Langley on the line. Roberts said the Blue Devils came out of the gates quickly with a 3-0 lead over Kamloops after the first period. The second period saw the Quesnel team take a 6-0 lead into the third, but penalties started to pile on late in the middle frame, resulting in a slow start to the third. Kamloops popped three quick goals to start the third and draw within three, but the Blue Devils expanded their lead to 7-3 shortly after, enough to advance to the finals. Roberts added that the Blue Devils took on a 13-man Langley squad in the finals, with just eight skaters and a goalie. Langley’s speed and team play proved difficult to contain, as the team opened the scoring five minutes into the first period and went on to claim a 6-1 victory. “More important than a silver medal on the ice is the fact that this tournament brought us closer together off the ice,” Roberts said. “When you see kids gelling at the hotel or at team dinner, those are the intangibles that turn us from hockey players into a hockey team.” Roberts also praised the team’s effort throughout the weekend, pointing to the work ethic that helped the Blue Devils reach the championship game. “As a coaching staff, we couldn’t be more proud of the work ethic that we displayed over the weekend. When you think of Quesnel, you think blue-collar and that’s exactly what got us to the finals,”
